candidate.long_definition: AI — short for artificial intelligence — is the umbrella name for software that does work that used to need a person. The kind of AI most people use today (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot) is good with language: reading, writing, summarizing, explaining, brainstorming. Older tools called "AI" were much narrower (a chess program, a spell-checker); today's AI is broad and conversational, which is why it's suddenly in the news, in products, and in district meetings.
candidate.why_it_matters: When a vendor pitch, a news story, or a student says "the AI said..." or "AI will change teaching," knowing what AI actually means lets you cut through the hype and ask the real question on the tech committee: which AI, doing what specifically.
candidate.example_in_sentence: A student admitted they used AI to draft their lab report conclusion.

candidate.long_definition: a calculated column adds a new column to a table in your data model, where the value in each row is figured out by a small formula (written in a language called DAX) when the data is loaded. once calculated, the value sits in the row like any other piece of data. this is different from a measure, which recomputes on the fly as the user filters or slices the report.
candidate.why_it_matters: a calculated column is computed once per row and frozen into the table. a measure recalculates every time filters change. mixing them up is the classic Power BI mistake — using a column where you needed a measure gives you totals that just sit there when someone slices the report.
candidate.example_in_sentence: we used a calculated column for customer segment because the value never changes once the row is loaded.

candidate.long_definition: a calculated column adds a new column to a table in the data model, where the value for each row is figured out once using a formula (written in a Power BI formula language called DAX) and then stored. it's different from a measure, which is a formula that gets recalculated on the fly depending on what the user is filtering or looking at in the report.

candidate.long_definition: a cookie is a small piece of data a website asks your browser to hold onto. the browser automatically sends it back to that same site on every later request, so the site can recognize you — remember you're logged in, remember your preferences, or track your activity. because cookies ride along silently, they're convenient for staying signed in but also need careful security settings.

candidate.long_definition: When you see a model described as "70B" or "405B," the "B" means billion parameters. Parameters are the internal settings the model adjusted during training — billions of tiny numerical dials that together encode what it knows. More parameters generally mean better answers but slower responses and higher cost each time you use it. The biggest open models (Llama 405B) and frontier models (Claude, GPT-5) sit in the hundreds of billions of parameters.
candidate.why_it_matters: Product names like "GPT-5," "Claude Opus 4.7," "Gemini 2.5 Pro," or "Llama 405B" start to make sense once you know the "B" is billions of parameters. It is the simplest rough gauge of a model's heft, though parameter count alone does not fully predict quality.
candidate.example_in_sentence: Llama 3 70B has 70 billion parameters — smaller than Claude but light enough to run on a laptop.

candidate.long_definition: encryption scrambles readable data into gibberish using a key. only someone with the right key can turn it back into readable form. it protects data moving across a network (like a web browser talking to a server over HTTPS) and data sitting in storage (like a backup drive in a closet).
candidate.why_it_matters: this is the difference between a stolen laptop full of patient records being a crisis and being a non-event. when IT says traffic is "protected in transit" or a backup is "safe to store," encryption is the mechanism doing the work. the flip side: lose the key and the data is gone for good.
candidate.example_in_sentence: IT reassured the unit that even if a workstation gets stolen, encryption keeps the chart data unreadable without the key.

candidate.long_definition: encryption scrambles readable data into gibberish using a key, so only someone with the matching key can turn it back into something readable. it protects data moving across a network (like a website session) and data sitting in storage (like a backup file). without the key, the scrambled version is useless.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is what makes a stolen laptop or a lost backup drive a non-event instead of a patient-data breach. when the help desk says traffic is "protected in transit" or a backup is "safe to store," encryption is the mechanism doing the work. the flip side: if the key is lost, the data is gone for good too.

candidate.long_definition: encryption scrambles readable data into gibberish using a key. only someone with the matching key can unscramble it back. it protects data moving across the internet (the lock icon on HTTPS websites) and data sitting in storage, like a backup drive. no key, no readable data — even for the people who built the system.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is the difference between a stolen district laptop being a real crisis and being a shrug. when a vendor says student data is "protected in transit" or backups are "encrypted at rest," this is the actual mechanism. the flip side worth asking about: if they lose the key, the data is gone for good — so key management matters as much as the encryption itself.

candidate.long_definition: an HTTP header is extra information attached to a web request or response, separate from the main content. headers can say things like what format the sender expects back, what login token proves who's asking, whether the answer is allowed to be reused later, or where the request came from. think of it like the label stapled to a prescription bag: the pills are the main thing, but the label carries the patient name, the prescriber, the fill date, and the warnings the next person needs to handle it correctly.
candidate.why_it_matters: a lot of invisible web behavior lives in headers: which login token is being sent, what content type is accepted, whether a response can be reused from cache, which site the request came from. when something works on one computer and fails on another, a missing or wrong header is often the reason — which is why help desk sometimes asks about them.
candidate.example_in_sentence: the release notes said the pharmacy system now requires a new authorization HTTP header on every request so the server knows which store is calling.

candidate.long_definition: an HTTP header is a small piece of extra information attached to a web request or response, separate from the main content. headers can say what format the sender accepts, what login token is attached, where the request came from, whether the response is allowed to be saved and reused, or what cookie should be set in the browser.
candidate.why_it_matters: a lot of invisible web behavior lives in headers: which login token is being sent, what content type is expected, whether a response can be cached, and which site the request came from. when a tool works for one teacher and breaks for another, a missing or wrong header is often the reason — useful to know when IT explains an outage at a committee meeting.

candidate.why_it_matters: a lot of invisible web behavior lives in headers: which login token is being sent, what format the response should be in, whether it can be cached, where the request originated. when a tool works in one environment and breaks in another, a missing or wrong header is often the reason — useful context when IT is troubleshooting the new charting system.

candidate.long_definition: autoscaling automatically adds more computing power when a system gets busy and removes it when things calm down. it watches signals like how hard the processors are working or how many requests are piling up waiting to be handled, then spins up extra capacity to match. when demand drops, it scales back down so nobody is paying for machines sitting idle.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is how a system survives a sudden rush without the company paying for peak capacity around the clock. it also explains the lag you sometimes feel when a system gets slammed: the extra capacity takes a moment to come online before it can start helping.
candidate.example_in_sentence: the release notes said the claims processing system now uses autoscaling, so it should hold up better during the monday morning refill surge.

candidate.long_definition: autoscaling means the system automatically adds more computing power when demand goes up, and removes it when demand drops. it watches signals like how busy the processors are, how much memory is being used, or how many requests are waiting in line, and reacts to those numbers. think of how your med-surg unit flexes staffing: census climbs, you call in extra nurses; census drops, people get flexed off. same idea, but with servers instead of people.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is how a system handles a sudden surge, like every nurse on every unit opening the charting app at 7am shift change, without the hospital paying for that much capacity all night long. it also explains the lag you sometimes feel when things suddenly get slow: new capacity takes a minute to come online before it can help.
candidate.example_in_sentence: IT said the charting system's autoscaling should kick in at shift change so the app doesn't freeze when everyone logs in at once.

candidate.long_definition: autoscaling automatically adds more computers (or servers) when demand goes up, then removes them when demand drops. it watches signals like how busy the processors are or how many requests are waiting in line, and adjusts capacity to match.

candidate.long_definition: CDN stands for content delivery network.
